marrow__ANAT_CH42_Q015.takeaway: The first two posterior intercostal pairs arise from superior intercostal artery (costocervical trunk), not thyrocervical branches.
marrow__ANAT_CH42_Q015.displayText: Rib notching is produced by enlarged posterior intercostal arteries, classically in coarctation of the aorta. The incorrect statement is that the first two pairs arise from branches of the thyrocervical trunk; the source states that the first two pairs are branches of the superior intercostal artery, itself a branch of the costocervical trunk. The lower nine pairs arise from the descending thoracic aorta; because the aorta lies left of the vertebral column, right posterior intercostal arteries are longer. The source states that there are 11 pairs and notes that they supply the intercostal spaces to the costochondral junction.

rationales.a: Posterior intercostal arteries supply spaces to the costochondral junction.
rationales.c: Right posterior intercostal arteries are longer because the descending aorta is left of midline.
rationales.d: There are eleven pairs of posterior intercostal arteries.

marrow__ANAT_CH42_Q016.takeaway: Postductal coarctation recruits intercostal and superior epigastric channels to carry blood toward the lower limbs.
marrow__ANAT_CH42_Q016.displayText: In post-ductal coarctation, lower-limb blood flow is maintained by enlarged collateral pathways including intercostal and superior epigastric arteries. The source describes an extensive collateral circulation involving axillary and subclavian branches, internal thoracic arteries, posterior intercostal arteries and inferior epigastric channels. It lists several routes from the subclavian system toward the descending aorta or external iliac system and notes rib notching from enlarged intercostal arteries.

marrow__ANAT_CH42_Q017.takeaway: The left first posterior intercostal vein drains to brachiocephalic or vertebral vein; left superior intercostal usually receives veins 2–3 and sometimes 4.
marrow__ANAT_CH42_Q017.displayText: The left first posterior intercostal vein is not a tributary of the left superior intercostal vein; on both sides the first posterior intercostal vein drains into the brachiocephalic or vertebral vein. The source states that on the left the second, third and sometimes fourth posterior intercostal veins form the left superior intercostal vein, which drains into the left brachiocephalic vein; lower veins drain into accessory hemiazygos or hemiazygos channels.

rationales.d: The fourth may join the left superior intercostal vein variably.

marrow__ANAT_CH42_Q018.takeaway: The left superior intercostal vein drains into the left brachiocephalic vein; right superior intercostal instead drains to azygos.
marrow__ANAT_CH42_Q018.displayText: The structures marked A are the right and left brachiocephalic veins. The left superior intercostal vein drains into the left brachiocephalic vein. The source lists tributaries of the brachiocephalic veins including left and right internal thoracic veins, left and right inferior thyroid veins, and the left superior intercostal vein. It contrasts the right superior intercostal vein, which drains into the azygos vein.

marrow__ANAT_CH42_Q019.takeaway: Superficial epigastric and iliolumbar veins do not provide an effective IVC bypass in the source pathway; azygos and vertebral routes do.
marrow__ANAT_CH42_Q019.displayText: The source states that superficial epigastric and iliolumbar veins do not help bypass inferior vena cava obstruction: the iliolumbar vein drains directly into the IVC and the superficial epigastric vein drains through the femoral system. In IVC obstruction, collateral routes use azygos/hemiazygos veins and vertebral venous plexuses; communications also involve iliac channels and tributaries of the IVC, inferior/superior epigastric veins, internal thoracic veins, brachiocephalic veins and the superior vena cava.

rationales.a: Superior/inferior epigastric channels can connect internal thoracic/SVC and external iliac systems.
rationales.c: Azygos and hemiazygos veins form major thoracic collaterals around IVC obstruction.
rationales.d: Vertebral venous plexuses provide valveless longitudinal collateral routes.

marrow__ANAT_CH42_Q020.takeaway: Aspirated objects preferentially lodge in the right principal bronchus; its bronchial veins drain into azygos vein.
marrow__ANAT_CH42_Q020.displayText: An inhaled foreign body most commonly enters the right bronchus because the right principal bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical. The source states that right bronchial veins drain into the azygos vein, whereas left bronchial veins drain into accessory hemiazygos or the left superior intercostal vein.

rationales.b: Right brachiocephalic vein receives other tributaries but not the direct right bronchial-vein route.
rationales.d: Accessory hemiazygos receives left-sided bronchial venous drainage when present.
